## Exodus 7 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet."

- **God's answer to Moses' objection.** God is answering Moses' complaint that he has "uncircumcised lips" (Ex 6:12, 30). The force is: "You don't need to speak — you will act with divine power. Aaron will do the speaking." (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **"As God to Pharaoh."** Moses was made "as God" by commission and office — not by nature. He was God's vicegerent, an ambassador clothed with divine authority to command Pharaoh, control him when he did wrong, and punish his disobedience. Pharaoh would stand in as much fear of Moses as if he were a deity. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

- **Pharaoh had rejected Yahweh** (Ex 5:2: "Who is the LORD?"), so God would now deal with Pharaoh through Moses. Moses would stand before Pharaoh in the place of God, not only delivering messages but backing them with acts of power. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **"Aaron shall be your prophet."** The primary sense of "prophet" (Hebrew *nabhi*) here is "spokesman" — one who declares the mind of another. Just as Moses was to wait on God's direction, Aaron was to wait on Moses' direction. (Precept Austin, citing Constable and Cassuto)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

- **A bitter irony for Egypt.** Cassuto notes: Pharaoh considered himself a deity, yet Egyptian gods "have a mouth but do not speak." Moses, however, would transcend them — he would speak God's decisive words, and Aaron would deliver them. (Precept Austin, citing Cassuto)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

---

### v. 2 — "You are to speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go."

- **The chain of command.** Jehovah → Moses → Aaron → Pharaoh. Neither Moses nor Aaron was to add to or subtract from God's words (cf. Deut 4:2). God's demand remained unchanged and non-negotiable: "Let My people go." (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

- **The Septuagint and Vulgate** read "Thou shalt speak *to him*" (i.e., to Aaron), clarifying that Moses spoke to Aaron, and Aaron to Pharaoh. (Pulpit Commentary, cited via Biblehub excerpts)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/7.htm

---

### v. 3 — "But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt."

- **God hardens Pharaoh's heart — but not against Pharaoh's own desire.** Pharaoh had already revealed his hard heart when he refused the humble request of Moses in Ex 5:1–4. God now confirms and strengthens Pharaoh in the evil he already chose. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Three ways the hardening is described in Exodus 7–10:** (1) God hardened his heart; (2) Pharaoh hardened his own heart; (3) a general statement "his heart was hardened" without indicating cause. All three are ways of describing the same reality. (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

- **"Signs" vs. "Wonders".** "Signs" (*'othoth*) were miracles done as credentials to prove a mission. "Wonders" (*mophthim*) were miracles generally — producing astonishment and awe. The plagues ultimately point to God's sovereignty superseding Pharaoh's. (Ellicott; Precept Austin)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm | https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

- **Romans 1 parallel.** Guzik notes that God can do the same today: when people persist in rebellion, God may "give them up" to the uncleanness they desire (Rom 1:24, 28). Yet even as God hardened Pharaoh, He also gave him reasons to believe — if he wanted to. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

---

### v. 4 — "Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out."

- **God foreknew Pharaoh's refusal.** God was not surprised. Pharaoh's obstinacy would be the occasion for a great display of Almighty power, attracting the attention of Egypt and all surrounding nations. (Pulpit Commentary; Guzik)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/7.htm | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **"My armies" (KJV) / "My divisions" (BSB).** The Hebrew *tseva'ot* is a military term portraying the people of God in battle array — an orderly departure like regiments. (Precept Austin, citing NET notes; Gill also notes the 600,000 men divided into twelve tribes as twelve "fine armies")
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

- **Ellicott's grammatical note.** The Hebrew reads: "Pharaoh will not hearken unto you, *and* I will lay." No direct cause-and-effect relationship is asserted between the two clauses — they are co-ordinate statements. God is not saying "I am hardening him *in order that* he won't listen so I can judge him," but rather both facts are stated side by side. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **"Great judgments."** The plagues are not just signs but judicial acts of God — He is at once righteous Judge and Saviour. (Precept Austin, citing Cole)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

---

### v. 5 — "And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out."

- **The purpose of the plagues stated.** The ultimate purpose is God's own glory — that the Egyptians would acknowledge Yahweh's sovereignty. This fulfilled the prophecy of Gen 12:3: "the one who curses you I will curse." (Precept Austin, citing Constable; Guzik)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Not just judgment — an invitation.** Kaiser notes the miracles were also an invitation for Egyptians to personally believe in the Lord. Some apparently did, for a "mixed multitude" left Egypt with Israel (Ex 12:38). (Guzik/Enduring Word; Precept Austin)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/ | https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

- **Ellicott:** "That I am Jehovah" — i.e., the only really existing God, while Egypt's gods are "vapour, smoke, nothingness." Egypt was the greatest monarchy in the world; to discredit her gods was to discredit polytheism generally. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

---

### v. 6 — "So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them."

- **A turning point.** From this point, Moses' diffidence wholly disappears. Once launched upon his Heaven-directed course, he persevered without wavering. (Pulpit Commentary)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/7.htm

- **Gill:** The repetition ("did"… "so did they") is not redundant but emphatic — showing with what care and exactness they conformed to the divine will. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

---

### v. 7 — "Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh."

- **God goes against convention.** Aaron was the older brother (83), yet God made the younger brother (Moses, 80) more prominent. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Longevity and preparation.** The air of Egypt and the desert was favourable to longevity; Egyptian monuments show officials active after age 100. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Gill:** These were men of wisdom and prudence, of sedate and composed countenances, fit to appear before a king. Stephen confirms Moses' age in Acts 7:23, 30. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

- **Guzik:** "This is retirement age for many, but Moses knew that God's will was more important than retirement."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

---

### v. 9 — "When Pharaoh tells you, 'Perform a miracle,' you are to say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh,' and it will become a serpent."

- **Pharaoh would demand credentials.** Ellicott suggests Pharaoh may have heard of the miracles done before the Israelite elders (Ex 4:30) and was curious — or may have thought his magicians could outdo them. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **A different Hebrew word.** In Ex 4:3 the staff became a *nachash* (serpent/snake). Here the word is *tannin* — often translated "dragon," "great serpent," or "crocodile." The crocodile was a symbol of Egypt itself (cf. Ps 74:13; Ezek 29:3). (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Gill:** The Septuagint translates it "dragon." The crocodile was frequent in the Nile — where Hebrew infants had been cast — and was itself an Egyptian deity. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

---

### vv. 11–12 — "Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts… But Aaron's staff swallowed up the other staffs."

- **Real demonic power, not mere trickery.** Guzik argues this was not mere magic but dark, demonic power producing what at least appeared to be miracles. Satan can produce "lying wonders" (2 Thess 2:9–10). Yet miracles can prove something is supernatural but cannot prove something is *true*. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Ellicott takes a more naturalistic view.** The magicians were "merely persons acquainted with many secrets of nature not generally known, and trained in tricks of sleight-of-hand and conjuring." The serpent trick may have been a well-known Egyptian snake-charming technique where a charmed serpent is made to look like a stick, then "disenchanted." (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Gill notes two views.** Some (like Josephus) say the serpents only *seemed* to appear; others think Satan actually removed the rods and substituted real serpents. Either way, Aaron's rod swallowing theirs demonstrated God's superior power. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

- **Jannes and Jambres.** The Targum of Jonathan names two of the magicians — Jannes and Jambres — names Paul confirms in 2 Tim 3:8. (Gill; Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Spurgeon preached "The Power of Aaron's Rod"** on this passage, using it to show that God's power "swallows up" our idols and sins. (Guzik/Enduring Word, citing Spurgeon)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

---

### v. 13 — "Still, Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said."

- **Ellicott's translation note (important).** The KJV "He hardened Pharaoh's heart" is a mistranslation. The Hebrew verb here is intransitive: "Pharaoh's heart hardened itself" — i.e., Pharaoh's heart was the subject, not the object of hardening. Ellicott says it is "essential to the idea of a final penal hardening that in the earlier stages Pharaoh should have been left to himself." (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Gill notes alternative readings:** Some render it "notwithstanding the heart of Pharaoh was hardened" or "therefore his heart was hardened." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

---

### vv. 14–15 — "Pharaoh's heart is unyielding… Go to Pharaoh in the morning as you see him walking out to the water."

- **Why the water?** Multiple suggestions from the commentators:
  - Pharaoh went out for morning ablutions/devotions — the Nile was an object of superstitious reverence, the patron deity of Egypt. (JFB, via StudyLight excerpts)
  - Perhaps to bathe, like the princess who saved Moses (Ex 2:5). (Ellicott)
  - Perhaps to observe the rising of the Nile (in June–July) to gauge the coming harvest. (Gill, citing Aben Ezra)
  - Perhaps to worship the Nile itself as a god. Theodoret and Athanasius both attest that Egyptians worshipped the Nile. (Gill)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **The rod that was turned to a serpent** is to be carried as a terror to Pharaoh — on sight of it, he would remember what had happened and fear further wonders. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

---

### vv. 17–18 — "By this you will know that I am the LORD. Behold, with the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn to blood."

- **"By this you shall know that I am the LORD."** Pharaoh had asked "Who is the LORD?" (Ex 5:2). God now answers by demonstrating His power over the Nile — Egypt's lifeline and god. (Guzik/Enduring Word; Gill)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/ | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

---

### vv. 19–21 — The First Plague: Water Turned to Blood.

- **Not a natural phenomenon.** Some propose a naturalistic explanation (red earth during high flood carrying organisms that kill fish). But if merely natural, Pharaoh would scarcely be impressed. Even if God used natural mechanisms, the timing and character were from His hand alone. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Ellicott disagrees with naturalistic views.** The natural discolorations of the Nile do not kill fish or render the water undrinkable. This was a true miracle — the water was made to have "all the qualities and appearance of blood." (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Judgment on Egyptian religion.** The Nile itself was virtually worshipped as a god. Specifically:
  - **Khnum** — guardian of the Nile, shown unable to protect his territory.
  - **Hapi** — the spirit of the Nile, brought low.
  - **Osiris** — thought to have the Nile as his bloodstream; in this plague he "truly bled."
  - Three species of Nile fish were also sacred. (Ellicott; Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Retaliatory punishment.** As the Egyptians had made the Nile the means of destroying Hebrew infants (Ex 1:22), so that Hebrew parents loathed to drink from it as if stained with blood, now the Nile is made undrinkable for the Egyptians by being turned to blood. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **The Ipuwer Papyrus.** Guzik notes an Egyptian papyrus from this general period (Ipuwer 2.10) that actually says the Nile was blood and undrinkable, and that servants left their masters — a possible extra-biblical corroboration. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Plagues grouped in threes.** Guzik notes the first nine plagues are grouped in threes. In each triad, the first two come with warning and a call to repentance; the third in each set comes without warning. The tenth (death of the firstborn) stands in a class by itself. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **"All the waters… even in vessels of wood and stone."** Ellicott praises the author of Exodus for showing "very exact knowledge of the Egyptian water system." The Nile water was stored in tanks/cisterns of wood or stone in homes to let sediment settle. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

---

### v. 22 — "But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts."

- **A small-scale imitation.** The magicians could not replicate the plague on a large scale. They dug wells (v. 24), found fresh water, and turned that small quantity red — perhaps by sleight-of-hand or by substituting blood. This satisfied Pharaoh, who was "probably easy to satisfy." (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **A telling irony.** The magicians should have turned the bloody river clean again if they truly had power. They didn't — because, as Meyer observed, "Alleviation of human suffering is no part of the programme of the devil or his agents." Satan can bring supernatural destruction but not goodness. (Guzik/Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

---

### v. 23 — "Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart."

- **Pharaoh was supplied with well water.** He probably drank wine or other liquids, and well water (however brackish) sufficed for his ablutions. So he dismissed the plague as a slight matter unworthy of much thought. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

---

### v. 24 — "All the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink."

- **Wells in the alluvium.** Wells could be sunk anywhere in the Nile Valley and would yield water — though brackish and unpalatable due to nitre in the soil. The water obtained was probably in the ground before the miracle and not made subject to it. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

---

### v. 25 — "And seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile."

- **The longest plague duration.** This first plague lasted seven days — longer than any other — because Pharaoh made no submission at all. Since he obtained sufficient water for his own purposes, he "thought little of its continuance." (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **"Seven full days."** Ellicott says this phrase marks the duration specifically. The plague was perhaps, of all, "the most nauseous and disgusting" if not the most destructive. (Ellicott)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Calvinist View on the Hardening (vv. 3, 13)

- **John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist):** Emphasises the absolute sovereignty of God in hardening. He argues directly against the common claim that "God's hardening doesn't start until later plagues, as a response to Pharaoh's own self-hardening." Piper points to Ex 4:21 and 7:3 — God declared He *would* harden Pharaoh's heart *before Moses ever arrived in Egypt*. Even when the text says "Pharaoh hardened his heart" or "his heart was hardened," it is always "as the LORD had said" — and what He had said was "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." For Piper, this means behind all "self-hardening" and "being hardened" stands the sovereign plan of God. Paul draws this out in Rom 9:18: "He has mercy on whomever He wills, and He hardens whomever He wills."
  — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-hardening-of-pharaoh-and-the-hope-of-the-world

- **Ellicott (Anglican) offers a different nuance on v. 13.** He insists the verb in v. 13 is intransitive — "Pharaoh's heart hardened itself" — and argues that it is "essential to the idea of a final penal hardening that in the earlier stages Pharaoh should have been left to himself." This reflects a more Arminian/Anglican approach where God's active hardening comes only after persistent human self-hardening.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Guzik (broadly evangelical/charismatic) takes a middle position.** God did not harden Pharaoh against Pharaoh's own desire; God confirmed and strengthened Pharaoh in the evil he already chose. Pharaoh revealed his heart in Ex 5:1–4 when he first refused. God's hardening is judicial — giving Pharaoh over to what he already wanted (Rom 1:24, 28).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

### Pentecostal / Charismatic on the Magicians' Power (vv. 11–12, 22)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Explicitly teaches that the magicians' enchantments were "dark, demonic power" — real supernatural miracles from Satan's hand, not mere trickery. He cites 2 Thess 2:9–10 and notes that "miracles can prove that something is supernatural, but they cannot prove that something is true."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-7/

- **Ellicott (older, pre-Pentecostal):** Takes the view that the magicians were "merely persons acquainted with many secrets of nature not generally known, and trained in tricks of sleight-of-hand and conjuring." The serpent trick was "well known to Egyptian serpent-charmers in all ages."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/7.htm

- **Gill (Baptist, 18th century):** Notes both views — some say the serpents only *seemed* to appear (Josephus), others that Satan actually substituted real serpents. He does not firmly decide.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/7.htm

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

I was unable to fetch pages from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org due to search/fetch limits. However, Precept Austin quotes the NET Bible notes at several points:
- On v. 1: Moses was to be "like God" to Aaron, and a "prophet" was one who spoke for God — an idea "with which Moses and Aaron and the readers of Exodus are assumed to be familiar."
- On v. 4: "lay My hand" is a "strong anthropomorphism to depict God's severest judgment on Egypt."
- On v. 5: By the time the exodus took place, the Egyptians would have "known" the name Yahweh — "probably hearing it more than they wished."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-7-commentary

## Summary of Key Themes Across the Chapter

1. **God's patience with Moses.** Despite Moses' repeated objections and outburst at the end of chapter 6, God does not chastise him — He simply gives fresh instructions and recommissions him (v. 1).
2. **The hardening of Pharaoh's heart.** This is the central theological tension of the chapter. Traditional readings range from full divine sovereignty (Piper/Reformed) to divine confirmation of human choice (Guzik) to initial self-hardening only later confirmed by God (Ellicott).
3. **God's superiority over Egypt's gods.** The serpent/crocodile miracle and the first plague both target Egyptian deities. The Nile — worshipped as a god — is shown to be under Yahweh's total control.
4. **Judgment as revelation.** The plagues are not arbitrary punishments but purposeful displays so that "the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD" (v. 5). Judgment serves God's missionary purpose of making His name known among the nations.
5. **Obedience as the proper response.** After their earlier hesitation, Moses and Aaron now obey "just as the LORD commanded" (vv. 6, 10, 20). This phrase becomes a refrain marking their transformation.
